pool.prompt: Which type of make-ready conflict occurs at the midpoint of a span rather than at a pole?
choices: Transfer conflict — existing cable must move to a new hook position at the pole

Midspan conflict — an existing cable's sag at the center of the span creates insufficient clearance for the new cable, even though the attachment heights at both end poles are acceptable; the conflict point is in the air between poles, and resolution typically requires re-tensioning the existing cable or shortening the span
Splice conflict — a cable must be spliced because it has no remaining slack
Grounding conflict — a cable lacks proper bonding at the pole
pool.explanation: A midspan conflict is distinctive because the pole-attachment heights on each end of the span can be fully compliant while the sag behavior in between still creates a clearance problem — this is why a make-ready survey needs to check the entire span, not just the pole attachment points, connecting directly to the T05.L02/L07 principle that clearance must be verified at midspan, not just at the pole.

pool.prompt: Your field survey finds 5 poles where an existing cable must be transferred to a new bolt position (no splicing required) and 1 pole where a telephone cable must be spliced because all its slack is deployed. Under OTMR, which poles can your contractor handle in one visit?
choices: All 6 poles — OTMR covers all comm-space make-ready regardless of splicing

The 5 transfer poles only — transfers with no splicing are simple make-ready (OTMR-eligible per 47 CFR 1.1411), while splicing is explicitly complex make-ready requiring the affected attacher's own crew via the traditional multi-party process; the splice pole runs in parallel on that separate track
None of the 6 poles — any pole with any conflict elsewhere on the route disqualifies the entire application from OTMR
Only the splice pole, since it's the highest-priority conflict
pool.explanation: OTMR's simple-make-ready scope specifically excludes splicing — the 5 no-splice transfer poles qualify for the OTMR contractor's single-visit process, while the 1 splice-required pole falls to the incumbent telephone company's own crew via the traditional multi-party process, consistent with the simple-vs-complex distinction covered in T05.L09.
pool.citation: 47 CFR 1.1411 — reused from the T01 research pass's independent verification.

pool.prompt: When a new attacher's arrival requires an existing (incumbent) attacher to move their cable, who typically pays for the incumbent's cable transfer?
choices: The pole owner pays, since it's their responsibility to maintain orderly attachment placement

The new attacher pays — under FCC rules and standard joint-use agreements, the party triggering the need for make-ready (the new attachment) is responsible for the associated make-ready costs, including paying for incumbents to move their existing cables to make room, even though the incumbent didn't cause the conflict
The incumbent pays, since they're the ones physically performing the cable move
Costs are always split 50/50 between the new attacher and the incumbent regardless of circumstances
pool.explanation: The 'cost causer pays' principle is standard in joint-use economics: the new attacher, whose arrival triggers the need to make room, bears the make-ready cost — including paying incumbents to move their own existing cables — which is why make-ready cost is a critical, often underestimated variable in aerial build economics.

pool.prompt: On a large multi-pole project with a mix of OTMR-eligible and complex make-ready poles, what is the correct project-management approach for minimizing total schedule time?
choices: Wait for all complex make-ready poles to fully resolve before submitting any OTMR-eligible applications, to keep the project simple to track

Run OTMR-eligible make-ready and complex make-ready applications IN PARALLEL from the start — filing both processes simultaneously (rather than waiting for one to finish before starting the other) lets OTMR sections complete make-ready and begin construction while the complex poles are still working through the traditional multi-party process, avoiding weeks of wasted schedule time
Cancel all complex make-ready poles from the route to avoid the multi-party process entirely
Only pursue OTMR-eligible make-ready; complex make-ready poles should always be excluded from a project's scope
pool.explanation: This is the same parallel-processing principle established in T05.L09 (and echoed in T09.L10's permit critical-path lesson): running the two distinct make-ready tracks concurrently from the start avoids the schedule waste of sequencing them, since OTMR-eligible sections can proceed to construction independently while complex poles work through their own (typically longer) process.

pool.prompt: A route has a pole where make-ready involves an unresolvable midspan conflict requiring a full re-route, with an estimated cost far exceeding the project's per-pole budget threshold. What project-management response does this scenario call for?
choices: Proceeding automatically regardless of cost, since any identified make-ready must always be completed as originally planned

A design hold — triggered either by make-ready cost exceeding a defined budget threshold (a percentage of build cost, set per-project or per-company policy) or by an unresolvable engineering conflict requiring re-routing — pausing that segment for a design-level decision (alternate route, cost re-negotiation, or scope change) rather than proceeding on the original plan
Immediately canceling the entire project regardless of how small a fraction of the route this pole represents
A design hold triggered automatically anytime ANY make-ready cost exists on a route, regardless of amount
pool.explanation: A design hold is a targeted response to a specific triggering condition — either cost exceeding a defined threshold or an engineering conflict that can't be resolved within the existing design — not a blanket response to the mere existence of make-ready cost (which is normal on most aerial routes) or an automatic project-wide cancellation for a single problematic segment.

pool.prompt: Why does a make-ready survey need to identify midspan conflicts specifically, rather than only checking clearance and separation at each pole's attachment point?
choices: It doesn't need to — pole-attachment-point checks are always sufficient to guarantee full-span compliance

Because differential sag behavior between conductors (different weights, tensions, or materials) can shrink clearance or separation to a non-compliant level somewhere along the span even when both end-pole attachment points are individually compliant — the same principle established for Rule 232 clearance (T05.L02) and Rule 235 separation (T05.L03) applies directly to make-ready conflict identification
Midspan conflicts are purely theoretical and have never actually occurred in real OSP construction
Midspan conflicts only matter for underground cable, never for aerial cable
pool.explanation: This directly connects T05.L13's make-ready survey practice back to the fundamental clearance/separation principles established earlier in the course: because different conductors can sag by different amounts, an at-pole-only check can miss a real midspan violation, which is why a thorough make-ready survey checks the full span, not just the pole attachment points.

pool.prompt: A route has 10 poles: 7 simple (OTMR transfer only), 2 complex (require incumbent splicing), and 1 with an unresolvable midspan conflict exceeding the cost threshold. What is the correct combined project-management approach?
choices: Treat all 10 poles identically and wait for the single most complex pole to resolve before touching any of the others

Run the 7 simple poles' OTMR process and the 2 complex poles' traditional multi-party process in PARALLEL, while placing the 1 cost-exceeding midspan-conflict pole on a design hold for a separate design-level decision — three distinct tracks proceeding on their own appropriate timelines rather than one single blocking sequence
Cancel the entire 10-pole route because one pole has an unresolvable conflict
Force the midspan-conflict pole through OTMR regardless of its complexity, since OTMR is always the fastest option
pool.explanation: This synthesizes the full T05.L13 toolkit: simple/complex make-ready run in parallel (Q4), while a genuinely unresolvable, over-threshold conflict gets a design hold (Q5) rather than blocking the other 9 poles' progress — treating all poles as a single blocking sequence, or canceling the whole route over one pole, both waste the schedule flexibility the parallel-track approach is designed to capture.

pool.prompt: A new attacher successfully argues that an incumbent's cable transfer isn't strictly necessary if the new attacher instead accepts a tighter (but still just-barely-compliant) attachment position. Why might this trade-off still be a poor design decision, even if it avoids paying for the incumbent's transfer?
choices: It's never a poor decision — avoiding make-ready cost is always the correct priority regardless of other factors

A just-barely-compliant attachment position is a zero-margin design (the same risk discussed in T05.L02/L07/L12) — it leaves no room for measurement tolerance, construction variation, or future creep, meaning the short-term cost savings from avoiding the incumbent transfer could be offset by a real compliance failure discovered later, which would then require an even more disruptive and costly fix
This trade-off is illegal under all circumstances regardless of the specific numbers involved
Attachment position has no relationship to compliance margin of any kind
pool.explanation: This connects the make-ready cost-avoidance instinct to the recurring zero-margin design risk established across T05: a tight, just-barely-compliant position saves money now but leaves no buffer against real-world variation — the short-term make-ready savings could be outweighed by the cost and disruption of fixing a later-discovered compliance failure, which is why experienced designers weigh margin, not just immediate cost, when making this kind of trade-off.
